question: What dropout rate did the base Transformer use, and at which points in the network was dropout applied?
answer: The base Transformer uses a dropout rate of 0.1 [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, pp. 7-8, Section 5.4 Regularization][Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, pp. 8-9, Section 6.2 Model Variations]. Dropout is applied to the output of each sub‑layer before it is added to the sub‑layer input and normalized [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, pp. 7-8, Section 5.4 Regularization]. It is also applied to the summed token embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, pp. 7-8, Section 5.4 Regularization].
answer_raw: The base Transformer uses a dropout rate of 0.1 [P1][P4]. Dropout is applied to the output of each sub‑layer before it is added to the sub‑layer input and normalized [P1]. It is also applied to the summed token embeddings and positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks [P1].

question: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide the dot products by the square root of d_k?
answer: Scaled dot‑product attention divides the dot products by √d_k to keep their magnitude from growing too large as the dimensionality d_k increases, which would otherwise push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention].

question: How long was the big Transformer trained, in steps and wall-clock time, and on what hardware?
answer: The big Transformer was trained for 300,000 steps, which corresponded to about 3.5 days of wall‑clock time, and the training was performed on a single machine equipped with eight NVIDIA P100 GPUs [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 7, Section 5.2 Hardware and Schedule][Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 8, Section 6.1 Machine Translation].

question: Did learned positional embeddings beat sinusoidal positional encodings in the Transformer experiments, and why did the authors keep the sinusoidal version?
answer: Learned positional embeddings did not outperform the sinusoidal encodings; they yielded nearly identical results to the base model [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, pp. 8-9, Section 6.2 Model Variations]. The authors therefore retained the sinusoidal version because they hypothesized it would let the model extrapolate to longer sequence lengths than seen during training [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding].
answer_raw: Learned positional embeddings did not outperform the sinusoidal encodings; they yielded nearly identical results to the base model [P2]. The authors therefore retained the sinusoidal version because they hypothesized it would let the model extrapolate to longer sequence lengths than seen during training [P1].
